preregistered_as: TOP_PLAN Phase 3.2 ablation #4 (sample rate x seed cost-stability)
queries: first 40 templates; 39 completed (q21 excluded: certificate exceeds 20s)

columns.l_hat_qerror_median: q-error of the rate-scaled unbiased point estimate vs truth
columns.sound_lb_over_true_median: sound lower bound / true cardinality (1.0 = perfectly tight)
columns.lower_validity: fraction of queries with sound_lower_bound <= true cardinality

findings.cost_floor: A 25x reduction in sampling rate (0.25 -> 0.01) buys only a 1.44x reduction in cost (0.728 -> 0.505). The cost never falls below roughly half of executing the join, because only one relation is sub-sampled while the remaining relations are still scanned and joined in full. Cheapness cannot be bought by sampling less.
findings.guarantee_collapses_linearly: The SOUND lower bound tracks the rate almost exactly (sound_lb/true = 0.0101, 0.0500, 0.0997, 0.2486 at rates 0.01-0.25). At rate 0.01 the certificate is ~100x below the truth, i.e. effectively vacuous as a guarantee.
findings.accuracy_is_not_what_degrades: The rate-scaled point estimate stays accurate throughout (median q-error 1.07 -> 1.01). So lowering the rate does not cost accuracy; it costs the GUARANTEE.
findings.implication: Sampling less converts the instrument from a certificate back into an ordinary estimate -- while still costing about half of simply running the query. This is the sharpest statement of the cost/soundness trade-off in the paper: the sampling lower certificate is expensive precisely because being a sound certificate is what makes it expensive.
findings.validity_unaffected: Soundness itself holds at every rate (100% validity), as Proposition 1 requires; only tightness degrades.
